subtopic: REPARATION BY GERMANY-ALLIES CONFERENCE AT OSTEND.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPARATION BY GERMANY-ALLIES CONFERENCE AT OSTEND.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the 18th instant the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. du Tremblay) asked me a question with regard to a special conference of the Allies to be held shortly at Ostend to consider the financial question affecting the Allies. The hon. gentleman desired to know if the Government had been invited to attend that conference and if Canada would have a representative at it, to which question I gave an answer in the affirmative. I find on looking at the official records, however, that we have no official notification of any conference at Ostend. The conference which I had in mind at the time of the hon. gentleman's question is one which is to be held at Spa of which we have been notified, and to which we have been asked to appoint a representative. In response to that request we have appointed Sir George Perley.
Before the Orders of the Day are called may I inquire of the Government whether we are to have a holiday on Monday next, Empire Day,

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is proposed that we shall sit on May 24. We think that we could not better honour the day than to engage in our usual duties.

I should like to say that we who come from the West have travelled a considerable distance and are kept constantly at Ottawa, but we are asked to adjourn on many occasions to celebrate Holy days. Now I think we should at least adjourn over Monday to honour the festival that is dedicated to our Empire.

The reason I had reached the conclusion which I have just stated to the House was that a great many hon. members, particularly those from the West, had expressed to me their intense desire that the work of the House should be proceeded with as rapidly as possible. Some hon. gentlemen have been urging me recently even to sit in the forenoons and on Saturdays, and I thought that in line with that strongly expressed desire we perhaps would he sufficiently honouring this highly important anniversary if we proceeded with our usual work on that day. If, however, it is the desire of the majority of hon. members that we should not sit on Monday, I can only say that I am just as ready as any one else tn take a holiday and will offer no personal objection.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: At all events, I am prepared to leave the matter to the judgment of the House.
Question.

I think that the 24th of May is an almost ancient holiday with us. Those of us who are no longer young will remember the 24th of May as a great holiday of the year, and I certainly trust that we are still going to have duly observed the Queen's birthday, as the day is known to us.
Hear, hear.
Since my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) appeals on the ground of age I am afraid I will have to back him up.
Hear, hear, and we stand by you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In view of the opinion expressed toy these hon. gentlemen, who have had a much longer experience than I in public life, I will move:
That when this House adjourns on Friday, the 21st, it stands adjourned until the Tuesday following at Three o'clock.

Carried.

On the order for resuming, from Wednesday, May 19, the debate on the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I would point out to
the House that Rule 17C states that on Thursdays and Fridays when the Order of the Day is called for the House to resolve itself into Committee of Supply or of Ways and Means the Speaker shall leave the Chair without the question being put. I know that notwithstanding this rule, it is the desire of hon. members that the debate on the Budget should proceed. In order to facilitate public business it is desirable that the debate should be carried on over 'Thursday and Friday, and I simply point out that our continuing to-day without the Speaker leaving the Chair is not to be construed as a precedent.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. IH. M. MOW AT (Parkdale):	Mr. Speaker, if a lawyer and, worse than that, a lawyer without a brief, or not much of a brief, may venture upon a domain which really should be reserved to those members who make or who sells things, if that be the case, I should like to offer a very few remarks in this very interesting debate. I naturally at the beginning would like to add a respectful word of praise to those which have been uttered with respect to the mariner in which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) delivered his speech on the financial affairs of the country. The Budget Speech was characterized particularly by two features. The first was courage and the second completeness. There were some who had doubt as to the capacity of the hon. gentleman to be the Minister of Finance, he not having had financial experience, to carry out the duties of his office but we who know' him for many years in our home town-as His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales might call it-knew that there would be no mistake made in his choice for that position because we knew his natural ability, his capacity for hard v'ork and his never failing capacity for taking pains. It does not surprise us, and the country as a whole will approve the method and material of his speech.
In discussing tariff matters it seems to me that the countrj, and those who take an interest in public business are much	in the same position as	that	ascribed	by Julius
Caesar to France, " Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres "-our country may be said to have three divisions in respect to its people; first, sensible business people, who want to see good business and as little dislocation as possible; second, free traders

in theory and, third, political propagandists and partisans who do not care much one w'ay or the other about the business of the country provided things can be steered in the direction of their own political preferences.
I believe that in the last two or three years we have not been able to understand tariff requirements for the reason that our country is so diversified and the business of one part differs so much from that in the other. There is no man probably in the country who is versed in all the requirements of the tariff. I was forcibly impressed with this when, last year or perhaps the year before, the battle raged a bit in the corridors and smoking rooms in regard to tariff changes. I was impressed writh this fact very much and on behalf of those who honestly felt that they did not understand all the features of the question or the contentions which were made by the respective parties and contestants, I suggested that we should choose two or three from each side who were w'ell versed in the matter, one from the standpoint of the manufacturer and business man, another from that class of business men who are farmers and another from those who are consumers. The suggestion that this little debate should take place, not in Parliament but elsewhere was received very agreeably, but I found that the interest flagged in what might have been a very interesting debate and which would have given us a much better understanding of the question at issue. I had come to the conclusion that a number of men on each side had not themselves made up their minds very clearly as to just what was needed by the country. It was forced upon my mind in regard to this debate and the stating of the case that one party was afraid and the other daren't.
Then again I learned at that time of some facts which made me still more doubtful as to the general knowledge of the people, and of members of Parliament on the subject. There is in my constituency a class who form the vast majority of the employees of the great works of the Massey-Harris Company, manufacturers of agricultural and other implements. Last year I was told by one of these employees that the Massey-Harris binder could be, and was sold in the Northwest Provinces at lower prices than the American machines were sold for. Well, this I confess was news to me because it had been continually dinned into my ears, as well as, the ears of others, that we were permitting the exploitation of

the Agrarian class by keeping up the price of these machines. However, I found there was no dispute as to this fact. The gentleman that I spoke to said, " Yes, that is true to some extent and the extent he meant was that the Massey-Harris machines were sold cheaper than American machines- considerably cheaper in some cases-in the Northwest as far west as Medicine Hat. At that time, arid at that place, on account of the longer railway haul, the prices naturally became greater; but the prices mentioned were the prices to distributing points in the case of the American machines, but the price of the Canadian machines was the price of the machine actually delivered at a man's own station nearby. This, of course, was an important fact which, if true, would change the opinion of many upon this question because the ordinary man in Canada does not want to see an injustice done to any class simply because another class happens to have the predominant voice in public affairs. If it is a fact it should be stated, and should be known by the people. Then, on the other hand I was told in the city of Toronto of a manufacturer-the man himself did not speak to me but a friend of his to whom he had just spoken did-who turns out a very large output of a certain kind of machinery and this manufacturer said that day-it was but a very few months ago-that if he had five per cent protection on his business it would be sufficient for him to carry on and prevent dumping from other countries at certain times. But the duty on the goods he manufactured was not five, but thirty-two and a half per cent. Now I was convinced from what I learned that this manufacturer did not- increase the price of his goods by the extra twenty-seven and a half per cent, because he was an honest, respectable individual, and he shrank from charging the people a price which would more than repay him for his investment and industry. But there you are:	We do not know how many of that
well disposed class of manufacturers there are, or how many take advantage of an unnecessarily excessive tariff to exploit the business for themselves. I am quite sure that when the 32i per cent duty was imposed it was necessary for that particular manufacturer, but now just as in the case of the Massey-Harris Company, it is not necessary. Therefore it is essential that the tariff should be revised by competent persons, possessing a knowledge of the wants of the whole country and not merely the wants of the people in a particular section. Accordingly, I hail with gladness the statement by the Minister of Finance, which seems to me of the most definite kind, that in August the board chosen to revise the tariff would commence its sittings. I believe that policy will be carried out, and I am strongly in favour of it being done before we undertake to tinker with the tariff, or cut down or raise duties, when we have not sufficient knowledge as to what the effect of such action will be.
The Massey-Harris people-at least the gentleman who spoke to me,-said that the reason the company now required the tariff was because at certain times of the year- according to the harvest period in different sections of the United States-the concerns in the adjoining republic would throw over their machines into this country and, at a sacrifice, undersell the Canadian manufacturers, because it would not pay the former to take those machines back to the places from which they were originally shipped, owing to the cost of the long haul that would be involved. Now, of course, that is something that our manufacturers certainly need to be protected against. If that is just a whimsical, selfish action on the part of our rivals in another country to undersell our manufacturers even at a loss, it is obvious to everybody possessing ordinary business sense, it seems to me, that we should protect our own people by some tariff restrictions. As the harvest moves eastward, or northward-on account of climatic changes-from Tennessee and the southern states, I was told there was a vast difference in the price of machines; and it would be very unfair to allow the exigencies of trade and manufacture in one country to interfere with the legitimate profits of manufacturers in another.
Again, I am glad that there is no present reduction, or dislocation, of the tariff by reason of the fact that I have a local interest in the matter, namely, that in the last dozen or score of years there have been established in the constituency that I represent hundreds of manufacturing concerns from the United States who have come here necessarily in order to carry on their business. They have brought thousands of employees of the very best kind; they have invested in these manufactures in Canada millions of dollars; and a sudden dislocation of the tariff, such as might he supposed to result from the adoption of the amendment of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) would certainly disarrange business to a very large extent. In addition to that if tariff reductions were made suddenly it is not at all likely that the employees who

are engaged in these hundreds of manufactures although they have become friendly to the country, and have their homes here at the present time, would prefer to stay in Canada. The strong cords of home affection would doubtless lead them hack to the land from which they came if there was no reason for the further maintenance of the business with which they are at present associated here. For that reason I do not want to see a sudden closing up of this vast number of industrial concerns, and the sudden departure of so many employees. Therefore it will be understood by the members of the House, and it is perfectly natural, that I, at least, should object to -an unthought-out lowering of the tariff or a cutting off of duties just to suit a theory.
The political aspect of this question is interesting because it is so dramatic. The other night the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) stated his political creed on this matter, and I must say that to me it was surprising. For many years I was accustomed to follow that hon. gentleman, and to agree that what he did in the public interest was right; and during that time any changes in the tariff from the old national policy of our Conservative opponents did not seem to us to be very shocking. I was rather surprised at the confession that was made by my hon. friend. Perhaps because I was brougnt up in such a strict political school I thought it was very bad politics to admit anything which might be taken advantage of by one's opponents; but the confession having been made that the Liberal party of those days was really not a free trade party but a protectionist party, frees me from the secrecy that I would otherwise maintain, and permits me to say that I concur with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) who made this confession that the Liberals of those days did not, among themselves anyway, claim that they had materially reduced the protective policy of the country.
I suppose the reason was that they saw everything was going well and they did not want to make a change. But I am told, although I have not analysed the figures myself, that the net reduction in tariff from * the time the Liberal party came into power in 1896 until their defeat in 1911 was only about two and one-half per cent. So It cannot be charged against me that I am very much of a "change-about" if in sitting on this side of the House on account of other reasons I feel very little sense of guilt when I hear my leaders of those days now con-
fess that their views on fiscal matters are very similar to those held by my colleagues on this side of the House.
But another interesting feature in the debate last night will be taken notice of by the country at large-the speech made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMas-ter), who I wish was in his seat now. That was a distressing incident. The hon. member on account of his abilities had been chosen to lead the attack from the financial standpoint, and in many respects he did it very ably. But he has been dispossessed .-I will not use such a word as discarded which I hear some hon. members suggest to me- he has been changed, no doubt as the result of consultation, because it was felt that something else had to be done than support the very strong views expressed by the hon. gentleman in former years in favour of free trade. So his speech last night was really in the nature of a swan song. He seemed to think that the times were out of joint-anyway his nose was out of joint-and the lack of that enthusiasm which formerly characterized his speeches on tariff matters was most noticeable. He did not repeat the methods of former years, which he then thought would be popular in certain sections of the country, by moving for the reduction of duties on certain specific articles. Consequently we must conclude that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have discarded his arguments of last year, which they then supported very reluctantly, and have decided to take their cue from those whom they have set up as their champions in the present debate.
Last year we all remember my hon. friend took a supposed "consumer" into an upper chamber and proceeded to undress him. First he took off the consumer's boots and told us the duty on them; then his sox, his braces, his shirt-really it got to be such a delicate subject that had not the hon, gentleman noticed there were ladies in the gallery I am afraid he would have gone to the extremity of completely disrobing this poor consumer in order to tell us what duties he had had to pay upon his habiliments. But there is no disrobing scene this year, no attention is called to any particular article of wearing apparel, and although my hon. friend made an able -speech he did not talk with the vim that characterized him last year.
So we are left in this position: That the Government promises scientific revision of the tariff based upon information gathered from all over the country; while the amend-

ment asks for an immediate cutting down of certain duties. In other words, there is a difference of only two months between the two propositions before the House, and for my part I prefer a scientific revision rather than an arbitrary and immediate reduction, which, it seems to me, is proposed simply as a foundation for political speeches and appeals to the avarice of certain classes of the community.
Before I close, I think it is proper that I should say something in reply to the remarks made by the hon. member for Brome in relation to the Militia Estimates. He suggested that they should be cut down to the extent of $4,000,000. He did not know what those Estimates were for, what sort of training the money was to provide, or in what other way the money was to be utilized, but he desired to have that wholesale reduction made so that he could emphasize his view that pacificism is the proper belief for the people of this country.
I am quite sure that my hon. friend is not without a certain amount of political ambition, and in spite of the fact that his views are highly unpopular in many quarters, he does apparently hope to attract a class of people who will put the crown of leadership upon his brow. Well, there does not seem to be any one to dispute with him that leadership. If nay hon. friend desires by making those strong statements, which are based purely on the theory about the sinfulness and wickedness of preparing to defend one's country he will undoubtedly attract to his banner-if there is such a thing as a banner among people of that sort-all those who were deterrents to our war efforts, all those who funked in that time of national crisis, all those who were of no use to the country when she most needed their services. Well, if he desires to become the leader of that class and of all the "sissies" in the country, he is welcome to the honour and I think no one will be anxious to become his rival.
My hon. friend referred to the splendid war record of our soldiers. Undoubtedly they did well, and there were times when they were the spearhead of the Allied forces. But how much less mourning there would be in Canada to-day if the men who "carried on" at the front had had sufficient military training to give them the skill and caution which is so essential in warfare to save the lives of our fighters and to make their gallantry completely effective. They would have been entitled to just as much in the way of credit, just as much in the way of thanks from our people, but 164
they would have been trained to protect themselves, as unfortunately they actually were not, and as a result there would have been fewer mourning homes in Canada than there are at this. day. I hope that the mothers of Canada will not be led away by any such arguments as those put forward by my hon. friends who seem to think that simply because they desire to maintain a pacific attitude w'e shall be exempt from the attacks of others who are stronger and more aggressive. History show's that that is not a sound way of looking at it. My friends on the other side who come from French Canada applaud such sentiments to some extent, but they must remember that their forebears were not of that kind.

I leave the geographical question to my hon. friend. History will tell them that in the early days Canada W'as preserved to their ancestors by the fact that they were always ready for defence; when the conflict came the French-Canadians were always better prepared than their English-speaking fellow colonists to ward off the attack and to attain victory. Even though hon. members may applaud these sentiments to which I refer, I know that that feeling does not exist in Lower Canada, in the province of Quebec. I know perfectly well that if hostile ships should sail up the St. Lawrence and the people of that province realized that they must protect themselves in order to avoid slavery for perhaps one hundred years, they would be just as keen upon the adoption of compulsory service as w'ould the people of any other province.
My hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) spoke also with a certain kind of sneer about Imperialism, which he linked with Chauvinism. He evidently feels that when a man thinks that it is wise to stay within the Empire; wise to keep on good terms with the Mother Country and with the sister dominions, that that involves a [DOT]certain vice, a wrong state of mind which ill effects the condition of Canada. Well, many of us do not agree with that. We think that our future and our happiness consist in the continued growth of the British Empire; and if it is called Imperialism to try to keep on friendly terms with the Mother Country and the sister dominions, then we are not at all ashamed of being Imperialists. But I do not know why the word "Imperialism" should have been used in the same sentence with the word



"Chauvinism," which means exaggerated nationalism. But we find that feeling existing; we see it in my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) who is supposed to lead in that respect. I regret to have to allude to this, but I feel that it ought to be protested against; if it were allowed to go uncontradicted it would be a sort of admission that an improper kind of Imperialism really existed. The greatest Imperialist vve ever had in Canada was the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was a sane Imperialist; he did not believe in subjecting Canada to the control of any other country, but he always endeavoured to maintain good relations between the component parts of the Empire Sir Wilfrid Laurier more than any other person gave a start to the good feeling between the Mother Country and Canada, which resulted not only in friendship but in material prosperity, by the granting of the Imperial preference, despite the protests of strong protectionists, and despite a strong national feeling in some quarters. In doing that he did the greatest thing for Canada, in my opinion, that was ever done. Sir Wilfrid Laurier remained in power a long time, as undisputed head of the country, but it must be remembered that at times he was not able to appreciate or to understand the sentiment of the country. When he was in favour of maintaining good relations between Canada and the Mother *Country and the sister dominions; when ,he was in favour of those ideas which we Imperialists say we have, he was successful; but when on two occasions he failed to appreciate what was felt by Canada as a whole on these subjects, he was disastrously defeated. If this misrepresentation is to go on, why, we cannot help it; for my part, I desire to state unequivocally where I stand, and if that will help anybody else in the protest against the sneering at Imperialism, then I believe I have at least done something in favour of my country.

In all $276,000,000 was extracted from the pockets of the poor people of this country in order to keep up prices against themselves. I know of nothing that is more iniquitous or less consistent with the idea that we are being given from day to day that this Government is sweating, blood in order to help these poor men. Nothing of the kind is being done to-day.
Is it to be expected that the working classes, the ordinary rank and file, will have confidence in any Government which, will because they have the power, come down to the Houses of Parliament and take from the pockets of these poor people, who are depending on us to protect them, this enormous sum of money?
If the Government had kept control of it themselves it would not have been so bad, but what has happened? They appointed a commission of their Tory friends and those who are manufacturers and producers in this country. They called them together and said: "Go to it; divide this $276,000,000 between yourselves ; there will be no competition." Nothing could be more in contravention of the principles of responsible government than to step in and spend this money for no other purpose than to keep up high prices and to make it impossible for poor people to get the benefit 
of that competition in trade which would otherwise have been given to them.
In the further observations that I wish to make, it comes to me now to say something about the subject of Government ownership and Government management. In the line of Government management or expenditure we have this $276,000,000 for which we have no substantial return. I do not think it was even mentioned as an asset by the Minister of Finance in his Budget Speech. It may have been; I have not been able to read it all but I followed the hon. gentleman very closely while he was speaking the other day and I do not recall that anything was said about this $276,000,000 which we have so lavishly expended on these foreign countries-foreign to us, all except Great Britain-and for which we have nothing of a substantial character to show in return. I was going on to say, Sir, that we should cease from this idea of monopolizing everything in the hands of the Government. As we do put that monopoly in the hands of the Government we decrease and break down the ambition of ordinary people, having the right, the ambition and the power, to do things for themselves and who should not be interfered with by the monopolistic operations of Government. I do not know but that I had occasion before to quote in this House a philosophic statement made by Lord Macaulay a long time ago. I think this statement was made by him in 1830:
" Our rulers will best promote the improvement of the nation by strictly confining themselves to their own legitimate duties, by leaving capital to find its most lucrative course, commodities their fair price, industry and intelligence their natural reward, idleness and folly their natural punishment, by maintaining peace, by defending property, by diminishing the price of law. and by observing strict economy in every department of the State. Let, the Government do this; the people will assuredly do the rest."
That, Sir, was the advice given to the British people so long ago as the year 1830. I find, Sir, that that idea is not dead; I believe that it is a British idea. I find that recently Sir Archibald Williamson, P.O., was addressing a gathering of business men in London, and I have here his views as reported in one of the newspapers. It was put up to him that the Government should cease from interfering with business in England, that they should give a free hand to the people to look after their own affairs, and his answer to that statement was as follows:
At the earliest possible moment that that emergency legislation could be brought to an end, it must be brought to an end, and at the

earliest possible moment they could finish with Government control they must do so. He would only remind them that when the Government brought about certain restrictions it was not through folly or lack of consideration. They did not do that without'going into the deepest consideration and argument of the matter. Those who condemned them were not aware of all the .details of the case before the Government. He made bold to say that there was not one member of the Government who did not desire to get rid of the control which had been necessary owing to the war at the first opportunity. They could not spend five years in such a war with a complete interruption of all commercial life and economic processes and then find themselves able to resume at once pre-war life. If they looked through the Government restrictions in the recent Parliamentary Bill carefully they would see there was not one which any of the members of that association would not think necessary and useful. He observed with pleasure that the chief articles of their association stood for the value of individual enterprise.
The whole history of their country, which had been the greatest country commercially in the history of the world, but whose commercial successes had not weakened its idealism for high effort, had built up its achievements on the knowledge that exceptional individual enterprise and ability deserved exceptional individual reward. They must sweep away the crazy doctrines and muddy philosophers which told them that the best way to achieve the best results was to work on the aggregate of all the citizens, where the reward of the thrifty man and the idle man would be the same. Ever since civilization raised its head there had never been a community in the world which had prospered on that system, but greatness had always been achieved by following the exactly opposite system. Speaking for the Government, he could say they had definitely set their faces against these doctrines.
It was the view of the Government that the great businesses and commercial enterprises of this country could better be carried on by private individuals for the good of the whole in the manner which had been customary in the past. When the Government was met by threats from any body of men, that they would adopt the course of action which could only recommend itself to them because they were in a minority, the Government would never give way to them -never. That was the touchstone of their ability to apply democratic doctrines as they understood them. The nation was going to govern itself through a Parliament cltosen by itself; and it was for the nation alone to decide those great business Questions and array themselves against all those who threatened to impose the coercion of a privileged class.
That, Sir, is the idea given 'by this distinguished member of the British Government, Sir Archibald Williamson He carries out, although not perhaps familiar with the doctrine established and enunciated by Lord Macaulay, the idea that runs through the minds of the British people; and to-day in England they are getting clear, as rapidly as possible, of the notion that there should be any governmental interference with the enterprise of the British people. If it is good enough for the people in that
country it should be good enough in Canada, and this Government should give way at the earliest possible moment and carry out what is suggested here by Sir Archibald Williamson-that the people of Great Britain shall select their own men for their own purposes, and that a Parliament shall be established in Great Britain at the earliest possible moment that shall properly represent the interests of the country as expressed by the freewill of the people. Let. me remind this Government that they are not on very stable ground. Let me remind them that the position they occupy is not a very proud one. From the Atlantic to the Pacific they have received notice to quit, and still they are not quitting. They are over-holding tenants, and they are determined to sit until the sheriff or the bailiff turns them out. Let me remind my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) of the many notices to quit that he has received. He received one from Prince county, in Prince Edward Island. He read it and put it away, no doubt marking the date on the hack of it. He received notice from Carleton and Victoria, in the province of New Brunswick. In that case also the same process was gone through and the notice was pigeon-holed. From Kamouraska in the province of Quebec he received a very emphatic notice to quit. From the division of St. James in the great city of Montreal he received notice to quit; and, no doubt, instructed his clerk to put it in the same pigeon-hole. Then, Quebec East has most emphatically sent- notice, in the person of my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) that this Government-as far as the people of that constituency wrere concerned-had reached far past the end of their tether, and the sooner they left the better. Then we come to Timiskaming, and we have the distinguished stalwart from that county here as a notice to quit which has been already served upon the Government. I had the distinction of being up in that constituency myself. I was not trying to help my hon. friend (Mr. McDonald) who is now a member, I was trying to help in the election of another man, but one thing I did tell the people was this: The Government'-not by any will or wish of their own but sadly enough owing to death-had given them the opportunity to speak their mind, and to state whether they approved of the Government or not. Now, Mr. Speaker, I
wish to discuss the tariff, a subject which my hon. friends on the other side of the House say we are not dealing with in that careful and logical manner which its importance demands. All I have to say to those hon. gentlemen is that as far back as 1893 the Liberal party established a tariff policy, they have been following it ever since, and during the fifteen years that they had the opportunity to put it in actual operation they brought such an era of prosperity to our people as was never enjoyed before and has never been enjoyed since. We were placed in power in 1896 on our tariff policy; we have not changed that policy since.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I hear some hon. gentleman say "hear, hear." But that is the fact. We came into power in 1896 with the avowed purpose of giving the best possible fiscal conditions to this country, making goods free wherever we could do so, and giving help to industries where help was required. In that way, and without erecting a high Chinese tariff wall, we succeeded under the leadership of our great chief, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, supported by the Hon. Mr. Fielding and others, in giving the country an entirely satisfactory government. What we are saying to the people to-day is "You had a trial of us for fifteen years and you know what we are. We have a good many of the same men yet in our party, including the hon. gent'eman who was our financial leader during^ those fifteen years. If you are satisfied with the way in which we handled the affairs of this country for the fifteen years we were in

power, we ask you to give us another trial, and we assure you that the good faith, the ability and the integrity that characterized our former administration will be continued in our efforts to bring back this country to the same prosperous condition which it enjoyed during our fifteen years in office."
I submit, Sir, that no person who cares for the development of this country will ever lay down any hard and fast rule to continue any policy, however good, without change no matter what the conditions may be. We have no intention of erecting a high tariff wall. We are prepared to carry on as we did before, to deal with circumstances as they arise, and, we hope, with the same successful results which attended our administration in days gone by.
Can it be said for the edification of those who think that we still adhere to the old National Policy that we stole the clothes off the Tory party in 1896, and that we were only adjusting those clothes to suit ourselves year by year? I imagine, Sir, that in 1896 no man in the House of Commons of that day understood the National Police better than the late Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper, who was then the leader of the Opposition. Undoubtedly he would recognize the National Policy just as well as any of his contemporaries, and if the Fielding policy which Mr. Fielding introduced in his Budget Speech in 1897 was the same old National Policy, no person would have been more ready to take advantage of the situation than the right hon. leader of the Opposition of that day, aru point out that while Mr. Laurier~as he then was-and his friends were promising tariff changes, yet their Budget proposals failed to give effect to that promise and merely constituted an adoption of the tariff policy of the Tory party. But what- did he say? I invite hon. gentlemen to look at page 1258 of Hansard for the year 1897, where they will find that the Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper speaking on the Budget that was then introduced by Mr. Fielding, said:
I confess, sir, that I listened with the most profound astonishment to the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding. I did not suppose it possible, whether in one section of the Empire or another, for a great Parliament such as that which the Dominion of Canada possesses to have presented for its consideration a Bill of such entirely illegal and unconstitutional character. I have no hesitation in saying that you will search the history of Parliamentary Government throughout the British Empire in vain to find any parallel for the position in which we find ourselves in relation to the Budget speech of the hon. Minister of Finance.
Again, at page 1262, in the same volume of Hansard, on the same date, the same right hon. gentleman is reported as follows:
Now I listened to 'this most remarkable address with the most profound astonishment because it violates the -most plain, clearly-understood1, and well-known laws governing the Parliament of Canada. It was in antagonism with the constitution of the country, and in violation of everything that hon. gentlemen on either Bide of the House had a right to expect from a Minister of Finance.
At page 1291 of the same volume he is reported as saying:
The result is that this tariff goes into operation, and the hon. gentleman knows that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence, while hon. members gloat, vindictively gloat, over the destruction of Canadian industries. I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail, of those industries in the Montreal Gazette, where one manufacturer after another declared that their industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House was in charge of the fiscal policy of this country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted upon Canada.
That, Sir, is the pronouncement of the gentleman who was leading the Tory Opposition, Who was at one time Minister of Finance and at another time Prime Minister of this country. He understood the National Policy; if he was not its father, he was certainly posing as its godfather. I must ask hon. gentlemen, therefore, to believe that the National Policy to which he referred was not the National Policy ,which was introduced by my good friend .(Mr. Fielding) on that occasion.
Now, Sir, what has happened? We had the application of that policy for fifteen years. I Wish to repeat and to bring to the touchstone of Toryism at its best the judgment which they passed upon the application of that Bill which Hon. Mr. Fielding introduced at that time, and also the results which that Bill, when enacted into law brought to this country. The new Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in the Tory administration which came into power in 1911 looked oveT the scene, looked over the results, anxious to find fault, if he could; anxious to show that the financing of the Liberals had been bad; anxious to show that they had not kept faith with the people. He was brought here to curse the Grits; lie was forced to bless them. This is What he said:
Our Dominion continues to be the land of hope and promise to the homeseeker. During the last year, as before shown, our immigra-

tion from Europe and the United States reached an average of nearly a thousand a day, bringing their capital, their intelligence, and their energy to assist in the great task of developing the resources of Canada, and building up her nationality.	,
Much has been said in the past with which I am in accord as to the selection of immigration as far as possible with an eye to the quality and character of our future citizenship. Notwithstanding the large stream of immigration, labour conditions are good, and extreme poverty from any reason other than incapacity or direct misfortune is hardly known.
Under the favourable conditions which I have described, and with every prospect for their continuance, the future of Canada looks bright indeed. In the enjoyment of peace, plenty, and prosperity, her energetic, loyal and patriotic people look forward with hope and expectation to an ever great and greater future.
That, Sir, is the testimony of the leading finance authority of the Tory party when they came to pass judgment upon our handling of the Fielding tariff for fifteen years under Liberal administration. That is their testimony, and we are prepared to place that before the people of this country and say to them: that is absolutely true; perhaps it is not the whole truth, because the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) could have gone much further in showing the grandeur, the immensity of the growth of Canada during those fifteen years. But he said enough to justify the administration of the country's affairs during that period. We say to the people: To-day we hold the same policy; we have the same ideas; we act in the same good faith; put us back in power and the same good conditions will come to you that were brought to you before. That, Sir, is the position which we occupy, that is what we say to the Canadian people.
As to our policy generally, we have standard ideas for the good of the people as set forth at the convention held in Ottawa last year. We stand by the resolutions adopted at that convention. That is our policy; that is our standard. We are willing that our opponents shall criticise us in respect to our living up to these high standards that we have set for ourselves; that they shall measure us by what we have done on forpier occasions.
I do not think, Sir, that it is necessary for me to put on record any of the resolutions that were adopted at that convention. The resolution respecting the tariff was put on record yesterday; it has been read in the press of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I shall not detain the House by putting it on Hansard now. But I wish to read the tariff portion of the Farmers' platform to show the striking similar-
[Mr. McKenzie.!
ity between our own policy as enunciated at the convention and the policy as put forward in this booklet which I received a few days ago. I quote:
Whereas Canada is now confronted with a huge national war debt and other greatly increased financial obligations, which can be most readily and effectively reduced by the development of our natural resources, chief of which is agricultural lands;
And whereas it is desirable that an agricultural career should be made attractive to our returned soldiers and the large anticipated immigration, and owing to the fact that this can best be accomplished by the development of a national policy which will reduce to a minimum the cost of living and the cost of production;
And whereas the War has revealed the amazing financial strength of Great Britain, which has enabled her to finance, not only her own part in the struggle, but also to assist in financing her Allies to the extent of hundreds of millions of pounds, this enviable position being due to the free trade policy which has enabled her to draw her supplies freely from every quarter of the globe and consequently to undersell her competitors on the world's market, and because this policy has not only been profitable to Great Britain, but has greatly strengthened the bonds of Empire by facilitating trade between the Motherland and her Overseas Dominions-we believe that the best interests of the Empire and of Canada would be served by reciprocal action on the part of Canada through gradual reductions of the tariff on British imports, having for its objects closer union and a better understanding between Canada and the Motherland and at the same time bring about a great reduction in the cost of living to our Canadian people.
That is practically word for word the policy of the Liberal party; and I was pleased to find that the Farmers' party, the Labour party and the Liberal party are almost, if not altogether, unanimous on the idea of making Canada a good country to live in, a free country, letting nobody have any special privileges, but keeping all on an equal footing, and saying that while we are anxious to assist the manufacturers just the same as every other Canadian who is a good honest man trying to make an honest living, it is our intention to let nobody take shelter behind an unduly high stone wall, behind which he can defy competition from the outside and sell shoddy goods at high prices to the people of Canada. Our intention is to give every honest man in this country a square deal and an opportunity of making a success, but at the same time, he must produce the goods and sell them to the people at reasonable prices and to the best advantage of those who live in the country. That is the idea which we entertain and which we intend to carry out, and the people of this country will, I am sure, hear with delight that before long this Government will make up their minds to be manly and

strong and will come to the conclusion at long last that their tenure of office has been too long and that the proper thing for them to do is to give the people of this country an opportunity either to confirm them in their seats, if the people so desire, or on the other hand, to send here men who will have the absolute confidence oi the nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

Then, he made some criticisms of another expenditure. He said that the Minister of Finance and this Government had given to foreign countries credits amounting to $226,000,000; or, to use his own words, that the Government said to the manufacturers: "Here is $226,000,000; divide it amongst you," and that the Government
