The Government, realizing the necessity of maintaining exchange abroad and the importance of supporting the starving population of Europe, found it necessary to supply some credits in this country in order to ship out the foodstuffs required in Europe for the starving populations, and, in addition to that, to stimulate our foreign trade by sending manufactured articles abroad. My hon. friend stated that this item was not shown in the figures brought dc-wn by -the Minister of Finance the other day; that there was evidently no record of this amount of $226,000,000. He said: It does not show as an asset. In the figures brought down by the Minister of Finance and placed on Hansard the day-before yesterday, not ancient history-if he had read the Budget they could not have escaped his attention-are the following:
Imperial Government	$171,710,168.19
Other governments	 34,336,117.75
Then there is a miscellaneous item after said: It does not show as an asset. In the record, included in the statement of the assets of the country, this enormous sum he speaks of. Now, I turn briefly for a moment to the wisdom or otherwise of these advances. Here we are in Canada with a rarge quantity of goods that we are able to sell to the world. What is the condition of affairs throughout the world to-day? Mr. Speaker, the subject has been gone over ,so often that one hesitates even to refer to it foi fear of wearying one's hearers, but in the face of the extravagant statements of the hon. gentleman, who was himself a leader for a year of a large party, it is necessary sometimes to harp back to facts that are known, to use his own words, to every school boy in the country. There is Europe, devastated and largely incapable

of producing, while its credits are generally destroyed. We in Canada have goods to sell and desire to open up new markets and get a share of foreign trade. What -s more wise than that, so far as we are able to do so, we should supply credits to such countries as may be reasonably safe in the matter of repayment? To whom did we extend credits?-to Great Britain, Belgium, Greece and a few other countries, and in every c.-se it was a wise and judicious provision on the part of the Minister of Finance. There is only one matter for regret in connection with this question, and that is that it is difficult for Canada to extend further credits to these countries. I think it is unfortunate that we are unable to do so. My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) .also, apparently with much pleasure to himself, read what he called the death warrant of the Government, calling upon them to resign and go to the country, and serving upon them a series of notices. If the hon. gentleman will remember, he referred to one trip he made to the constituency of Timiskaming. He said:	"I made a
speech up there and I told the people there that whatever they did they should vote against the Government candidate. They might vote for a Farmer or for a Liberal, but whatever they did they should not vote for this pernicious Government." I presume that is the only speech he made there, but he took a great deal of credit to himself in the matter. Now, what was the result on polling day? In the town in which he delivered that address we find that the Government candidate received a vote of practically two to one against his opponent; and I think that if we desired to be at all selfish, we might express the regret that we did not invite the hon. gentleman to speak at other places in that constituency. If my hon. friend can take any solace out of the results let him. .
Last year the hon. member was in the position of leader of the Opposition, and how well we remember, in , the Victoria Museum, his standing in his place and holding out the light in the window to the Liberal-Unionists on this side. The latch string was hanging out through the door, and the hon. gentleman drew a homely picture inviting the Liberal-Unionists to come back. He has no word this year for those gentlemen; he turns to my hon. friends the farmers from the prairies and holds out a winsome invitation to them to come in and join his ranks. Why, he says, " there is no difference between our policies; our policy is just the same as yours;

we are all out for a reduction in the tariff;" but he says, " we must stand pat where we were in 1896." How my hon. friend will justify himself before the country in standing pat as he was in .1896 I do not know. I notice when he said that, that his chest expanded and his voice increased in volume, but when he was talking to my hon. friends opposite his 'brow clouded and his voice was tremulous and I could scarcely catch what he said. He was not so sure of himself on that occasion, but he followed the lead given by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and decided that he must hand out some sort of invitation, and therefore he gave the invitation to his farmer friends to come in and join in his policy.
Now, I should like to proceed to review briefly the attitude of my hon. friends opposite as given to the Bouse and the country in speeches delivered by the leading critics of the Opposition, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I think it is proper and desirable that we should know how hon. gentlemen opposite stand on this subject, because after all the way we judge as to the value of our hon. friends' criticisms is to measure them up and see whether or not the opinions expressed by their side all agree. If they do not agree then these hon. gentlemen can hardly expect us to accept them. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, who for fifteen years was Minister of Finance of this country and who speaks with a great deal of experience and authority, yesterday I think spoke with intense sincerity; and out of his years of wisdom, out of that fifteen years of ripe experience in the position of Minister of Finance, and from his life long experience as a Liberal, he gave his verdict on free trade. We cannot doubt for a moment that he had studied the question. He is an intelligent .man; he is a learned man, the editor of a large financial journal which speaks for the financial interests of the country to a large extent; and his words are worthy of consideration. .Speaking of free trade, he said, after stating what it was:
That is free trade, but it is quite possible that the best of principles may be carried too far; it is quite possible that men who believe in the general principle of free trade must recognize that there are conditions under which it cannot be applied.
My hon. friend from Brome has something else to say in the same debate, and on the same issue. Speaking from the
same benches as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen s, he cites a book written
by Mr. Keynese on why Europe may become free trade territory, and says:
That is the policy which the Liberal party aim at in the future. That is the policy which I wish to see adopted in this country.
On the one hand you have a learned and experienced leader on the other side declaring that it is impracticable and unwise to apply the principles of an abstract theory in practice; and on the other hand you have a pseudo-leader declaring that it is his intention to stand four square on the great principles of free trade, of which by the way I shall have something to say later on.
Then we have my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's enunciating some other doctrines -which certainly are in absolute contradiction of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite as expressed in this and in every preceding similar debate in recent years. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) took the full credit and responsibility of the dumping clause, an arbitrary, definite, protective measure and a measure that I do not for one moment criticise. We ought to bear in mind that hon. gentlemen who pretend to a certain element in the country that they are the friends and the advocates of the policy of free trade have no right to stand upon this doctrine which has been enunciated by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's.
But that is not all. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) takes a step forward and he makes another rather extraordinary statement, a statement that I, with all my Toryism, such as it is, would hesitate to make in this House. He says that not only is he in favour of a measure of protection but that the peculiar brand of protection he is in favour of is the bonus rather than the customs tariff. Bonuses and bounties are classified by all economists as constituting the most extreme measure of protection. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's to quote his words, says:
I would willingly help an infant industry, and as between protection and bounties__
Mark his words !
I think I would prefer the bounties.
That is from the lips of the leading financial critic of the Opposition, the hon. gentleman who himself moved the amendment to the resolution which I shall deal with later. Again I invite the attention of the House to a strange contradiction in

the attitude of his colleague who followed him a few hours afterwards and who referred to the statement of the Minister of Finance dealing with infant industries and the necessity of not killing or annihilating them by careless or reckless legislation. The hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMas-ter) goes on to say:
He speaks of legitimate industries. What are legitimate industries in this country?
Bearing in mind the attitude of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen s, this is what he says:
I will answer that. Legitimate industries are those which can stand on their own feet, and pay their own way, and Which do not require to be bonused by the taxpayers of this country.
On the one hand you have one leader (Mr. Fielding) stating that he prefers bounties and bonuses in protecting infant industries and on the other hand you have his colleague, (Mr. McMaster) ousted temporarily I believe, from the position of chief financial critic, saying that he is absolutely opposed to bonuses and bounties.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's not only was in favour of bonuses and bounties but he was in favour of mergers as well. Again I am not differing from him. I would pause to say t-hat in my estimation, and this has been my opinion for a great many years, so called mergers, combines or whatever terms you like, or large combinations of capital as applied to industry, constitute a wise and economical method of handling industry provided there is reasonable governmental restrictions on their operations so that they cannot impose their power upon the country in an oppressive manner. In so far as the operation is concerned I believe it is a sound and economical method of industrial control. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's comes out flatfooted for the merger. Can we not hear the former member for Edmonton, the Hon. Frank Oliver, from his place in this House, year after year, as I and many hon. members have heard him, hounding the Government because he said that it was, supporting trusts, mergers and combines? Today, here is his colleague (Hon. Mr. Fielding) who sat with him for fifteen years in the same Cabinet chamber standing foursquare for trusts, mergers and combines. That is the condition that we see amongst hon. gentlemen opposite. In the light of that attitude of mind, in the light of these statements made by these hon. gentlemen, /what construction are we to 
put upon the amendment which is before the House?
The hon. member for Brorne made the statement that he delighted to take Great Britain as an example and lead in his financial policy. In view of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in moving this amendment, I am going to invite the attention of the House for a moment to the last British Budget delivered only a few weeks ago by the Right Hon. Austen Chamberlain whom my hon. friend delights to follow. What was done in that Budget in the way of taxes? Compare Mr. Austen Chamberlain's action with that of our Minister of Finance. The British Government brought down their Budget and increased the taxes in connection with the postal service-we have a Bill on the table of this House to increase the charges in connection with the postal service. The British Government increased the taxes in connection with telegraphs and telephones. That is a Government institution over there and we as a government are not so deeply interested here in telegraphs and telephones. They increased the charge for .motor licenses, which service is controlled by the Imperial Government-we are imposing a new and enlarged tax upon motors in this country. I am sorry that my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) is not in his seat but I invite the attention of his colleagues, because this is 'included in their platform, to the fact that the British Government repealed the land values tax. They increased the taxes on spirits, beer, wine and cigars. One would think that they had been reading the proposals of the Minister of Finance of Canada. They enlarged the stamp taxes increasing the tax on cheques, notes, share transfers, receipts, etc. They made no increase in the income tax. We have made an increase in the income tax. They also have a business [profits tax, as we have. They have imposed a new tax on corporations in Great Britain. We last year put a tax on corporations, which has been in operation for a year and is being continued. These are new methods of taxation in Great Britain practically every one of which is included in the Budget before us to-day. Will my hon. friends opposite, in the few days to come, stand up in their places and advocate the complete wiping out of these proposals?
The hon. member for Brorne made a proposal also that I think should be reviewed very briefly because it should not pass without being taken notice of. He

stated yesterday that there certainly should be a direct levy on war wealth. He means a direct levy against capital. Is he justified in standing on this ground? He told the House that a Royal Commission in Great Britain had passed upon the question and that a Bill is about to be brought in. As a matter of fact Mr. Speaker, he is a long way ahead of the pace set in Great Britain in that regard. A commission, or a committee of the House, is, or has been, sitting on this question. They have not yet reported, .and the Chancellor of the Exchequer stated in his Budget Speech that he was not yet certain whether or not the matter would be taken up in the way of legislation. But there is a vast difference between a levy on capital in Great Britain and a levy on capital in Canada. The difference, which is fundamental, is this:	Capital	in Great Britain is very
largely of a liquid character. Great Britain has been for centuries the banker of the world, and there is concentrated in that country a great deal of liquid capital. During the war many individuals, for their firms, corporations and so forth, made huge profits, which came to them in the form of what I call liquid wealth. What is the condition of Canada? Nearly every firm, nearly every individual, that made money to any degree out of the war, have invested their profits in the enlargement of their plants. Investment was made by placing all their profits back in their business, enlarging their plants; and in very few cases -as far as I have been able to discover, and I have given the matter a great deal of thought-has there been any very large increase in what you might call liquid wealth. Now let us see? How would you assess or take this wealth? My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) was very silent on the question-he did not discuss it. He gave no indication that he had given it a moment's thought; he simply propounded it as a thing that would appeal to the popular ear. The taking of the war wealth ! How would you take the war wealth? Let us get down to something concrete! Here is, we will say, a large factory like the Poison Iron Works in Toronto, or one of the large packing concerns. These people made money, a certain amount of money during the war. But what occurred? Those who were engaged, for instance, in the manufacture of munitions, in almost every case put that money into new machinery, or extensions of plant, and there it is to-day. If we were to assess their wealth, so called, the only way we could secure any portion
of it would be by taking a portion of the plant, or forcing a liquidation of the plant. I will give a concrete illustration. I know of a firm-a saw-mill, a lumber company- with a capital of $100,000. They borrowed from the bank, $200,000 which made their invested and operating capital $300,000. Now when aeroplane spruce was being cut in large quantities this firm made a net profit of $100,000. You might say that was 100 per cent profit on the capital, and that they should pay a large sum into the treasury of the country. As a matter of fact, under the existing law, that firm is assessed at $64,000. Now, what is the result? The firm is faced with this condition: They have borrowed from the bank the last dollar of credit they could secure, $200,000. They are asked to pay $64,000 into the exchequer. They have not got it. Where is the $100,000? It is in extended plant, a new wharf, an increase of their machinery, the extension of buildings, and an increase of stock being carried in their yard. In order to pay the tax levy, or the assessment on their wealth direct, they would be compelled to close down and liquidate by the selling of a portion of their plant. I merely state that to indicate the difficulties facing those who take any stock in the proposal so lightly suggested by my hon. friend from Brome.
Now let me turn for a moment or two to the amendment, moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), and I think hon. gentlemen on both sides should give it the closest attention. What is the significance of this amendment, what does it mean? My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has moved that "all the words after, that (in the resolution) be struck out." Now what does that mean? It means this: That all the schedules, that all the proposed taxes, will be cut off supposing the amendment carries. There will be no such taxation imposed, and this revenue will not be raised-it will be abandoned. The amendment condemns the action of the Government in proposing this taxation, and repudiates the whole resolution submitted by the Minister of Finance. In other words, to make the amendment more direct and practical, hon. gentlemen opposite propose to strike out the ten per cent tax on luxuries, the fifteen per cent tax on automobiles, the twenty per cent tax on gramophones, etc., the twenty per cent tax on playing cards, the thirty per cent tax on patent medicines, etc., the $2 a gallon on liquors, the thirty cents a gallon on ale and beer, the $3 on champagne

They propose to strike out the provision for one per cent on sales; to strike out the increased tax on bills of exchange and promissory notes, and the tax on the transfer of.shares. They go even further-they prevent the imposition of an increased income tax. They stop the repeal of the seven and a half per cent customs war tax, and they prevent the putting on the free list of books and appliances for the blind. That is what the amendment means-it means a complete and absolute repudiation of the total proposals of the Government for the raising of revenue in this country during the coming year.
Now, what do my hon. friends opposite offer in place of that? This I submit, Sir, is a logical and proper question to ask. Not one single word has dropped from the lips of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, the hon. member for iBrome, or the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, to say what they propose to put in place of the Government's taxation proposals. My hon. friends repudiate and reject all the proposals of the Government, and this is what they propose to adopt in their place: They express a pious wish in the amendment that substantial reductions of the burden of customs taxation may be brought about. Now let us consider that for a moment. Here we are in Canada faced by an enormous expenditure. What does that expenditure consist of? An enormous sum for interest on our war debt; a huge sum for pensions; large amounts of money for land settlement; and then there is the cost of carrying on the ordinary business of the country. These are the purposes for which the Government is asking money from Parliament. We must get the money, and hon. gentlemen opposite know that themselves. The Finance Minister shows that he will he able to raise a large portion of this money-what he proposes will meet almost the total of the ordinary expendi tures-but he points out that in the fall there is accruing due somef $70,000,000 ol short term loans, and those of us who have given the matter any consideration at all know that next year, and the following year, 1922-3, there are other sums coming due. Is it not only wise but prudent on our part to make adequate provision to meet these short term loans? We must do so, or else go into the market and borrow with the result of enlarging our debt, increasing our burdens, and following a line of action that is not being adopted, I am glad to say, by any other country in the world of the standing of Canada. So, Sir, 
my hon. friends opposite, by their amendment-and I wish to make this absolutely clear; they know it, I presume, but apparently are ignoring it-repudiate every, proposal that has been submitted for the raising of this money. If my hon. friends opposite vote for that amendment, as possibly they will, then they repudiate the very measures that they advocate in theii own platform, a direct tax of one kind or another, and I shall deal with that a moment later. They not only do that, but they fail to submit one single suggestion of a concrete character to take the place of these enormous reductions that must come about. Is that the whole story? It is not, for there is this much further: They propose a drastic and a definite reduction of customs duty. What does that mean? Can they reduce the customs duty without reducing the revenue? Our revenue from that source is in the neighbourhood of $159,000,000. If they make any tariff reduction that is worth while-30 per cent would not be an unreasonable guess at what they are aiming at-it would mean $50,000,000 additional reduction. And not a single word as to what source of revenue is to take its place.
I invite hon. gentleman opposite to give consideration to this amendment, I invite them to give consideration to the absolute and imperative necessity of carrying on during this year and meeting some of the obligations to which I have referred. Surely we can fight out the points of differences on methods without absolutely abandoning the needs of the country; surely, Sir, we could produce to this House some suggestions which might be different from these proposals without rejecting the latter in toto; surely there is some merit in the proposals of the Government. I hold that those proposals, as far as we have been able to judge, have been received throughout the country with general approval, and I doubt if my hon. friends will get very much credit from the people in their efforts-which will fail -to land the country into the lamentable position which their amendment would produce if adopted.
We have heard a great deal during this debate about the Government not keeping faith in connection with tariff reform.- I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am independent enough and radical enough to criticise the Government if I consider it is derelict in. its duty-and I have done it when it has not perhaps resulted in any particular good to myself. But let us look at this thing fairly. Last year the right hon.

member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White), then Finance Minister, made a statement in 'his Budget Speech-a carefully prepared statement, in which he said, among other things:
Within a year conditions will, I hope, have become stabilized so as to permit of a general revision of the tariff.
And he wound up by saying:
My own view is that it might well commence in the fall.
My hon. friends opposite charge the exFinance Minister with having broken faith, with having made a promise which has not been carried out. But that statement of his was based on conditions becoming stabilized. Now, I ask hon. gentlemen seriously if ever there was a time in the history of the world when conditions were less stable than they are to-day-or than they were in January and February, because they have, I am glad to say, improved a little since? Was there ever a time in the history of this country, even during the Crimean War before Confederation, when the conditions were less stable than they were in the months of January and February? Exchange was so demoralized that the whole world was temporarily in a panic. The only thing that saved us from a serious panic in the United States and Canada was the fact that the Old Land, with its usual buoyancy, was able to ship to New York large quantities of gold in the last few months, somewhat temporarily, at least, stabilizing conditions.
But would any hon. gentleman suggest, seriously that this was a time to reduce the tariff? How could we reduce it, looking at it from a practicable standpoint? Could we take up the schedules covering the imports from the United States under the present abnormal conditions with exchange against us; or the schedules which naturally cover importations from France, or from Belgium, or from any of the other European countries where the discount against them ranges from 60 to as high as 90 per cent? While I am strongly in favour of a revision of the tariff, I think the Government would have been derelict in its duty had it precipitated a revision under those conditions. Not only would it have been derelict in its duty, Sir, but it would have attempted an almost impassible task.
My hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) quoted a statement made in 1911 in connection with a Bill then before the House to create a permanent tariff commission. That Bill was killed in 165
the Senate,-not by supporters of this Government or of the Government to -which this succeeded-, it was killed by his Liberal friends in that Chamber at the instigation of his friends in this House. He referred to that, and then he said that we had gone for eight years since and no effort had been made to appoint a permanent tariff commission. I again invite the House to give that statement consideration. Has there been any day from the 4th of August, 1914, down to the present time when a revision of the tariff was a practical measure? What would my hon. friends have said if in the year 1918, or 1917, or 1916, or even last year, this Government had stated to the House, "We propose to revise the tariff," Why, they would have told the Government Very plainly that it was out of its mind to attempt such a thing under the circumstances. There was not a day from the 4th of August, 1914, dowm to the present time wdien it v'as a reasonable proposition to attempt a revision of the tariff; and I very much doubt whether it will be possible within the next eight or ten months.
I am firmly of the opinion that the Government should surround itself with tariff experts. I know they have some already who are second to none, but I think they might perhaps enlarge this staff a little, and secure, as soon as conditions are reasonably stabilized, the fullest information. I think the Government could go this far: they could prepare the machinery which would undertake this investigation, so that when conditions become stabilized in the next five or six months this machinery could be put into motion and we might have some results later on. But for the Government to have undertaken this proposal at any time up to the present moment would have been unwise, impractical and injudicious.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to address myself briefly to what is known as the Farmers' platform. I approach this question not with any desire to be hypercritical of my hon. friends, but rather to draw attention to some striking things in connection with this so-called platform. First, however, I wish to say a few words to the members of that party in this House, which I trust they will receive in the spirit in which I tender them. In that platform they make a rather extraordinary and .sweeping statement, and I invite my hon. friends to consider this statement in the light of the additional experience, perhaps, which they now have. I am sorry the hon.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to go a step further in connection with this Farmers' platform. I find in it this clause:
That all corporations engaged in the manufacture of products protected by the customs

tariff lie obliged to publish annually comprehensive and accurate statements of their earnings.
I have no particular objection to a requirement of that kind. But what I do object to, and what I would impress upon my hon. friends who advance this platform, is this, that it is decidedly unfair, undemocratic and unjust to limit the publication of comprehensive and accurate statements of earnings to the manufacturers. Why the manufacturers more than any one else? Why should the manufacturers any more, for instance, than an operator of a grain elevator, or a large wholesale implement dealer, a coal dealer, a dealer in flour, in lumber or in other commodities commonly used by the people, be required to do this? Why should not these, as well as the manufacturers of the country, publish comprehensive and detailed statements of their earnings? In substantiation of this, and again to point out to my hon. friends that they are not coming before the House with clean hands in this regard, I wish to draw to the attention of the House some figures in connection with the operations of the United Grain Growers and subsidiary companies. There is a company, the stock of which is owned and controlled by the United Grain Growers, known as the Grain Export Company. It is a New York corporation and all of it3 stock is owned by the United Grain Growers' Company. This Grain Export Company has an authorized capital of $250,000, but its records show, and the sworn statement of Mr. Rice Jones, the secretary of the company, also shows, that the company had a paid-up capital of $100,000 and the balance of $150,000 was paid out of stock dividends. At this point I pause to bring to the attention of the House another clause in the platform of my friends, a clause which is very interesting in the light of this method of financial manipulation:
That in levying and collecting the business profits tax the Dominion Government should insist that it be absolutely upon the basis of the actual cash invested in the business and that no considerations be allowed for what is popularly known as watered stock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says,
"Hear, hear," and I agree wdth him absolutely. But the point I am making is this: If those gentlemen are going to include in their platform a statement of that kind, if in all their speeches, in the speech of the president of the company on the occasion of its annual meeting, and in the public speeches of my hon. friend from Marquette
fMr. Stevens.]
(Mr. Crerar), they are going to condemn the practice of creating capital which does not represent cash invested, then I say we are justified in reviewing the operations of some of their own companies. Now, I bring this particular company to the attention of the House. What is its financial history? Briefly this. It has an authorized capital of $250,000, of which $100,000 was paid up in cash and $150,000 was paid in the form of stock dividends. Had that been a concern in which, let us say, my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) or some other hon. member representing a manufacturing company was concerned, that would have been considered watered stock, and it would have been condemned as an unreasonable and unfair imposition on the public. It would be charged against the manufacturer as being an extortion from the people. But that is not all. I find in the sworn statement of the secretary the following:
In addition to the stock dividend of $150,000 this company paid to the parent company $300,000 in cash.
That is pretty fair earning. As a matter of fact, in one year's operation this Grain Export Company, with an actual cash investment of $100,000, made $500,000 of profit. I repeat to you, Sir, and I draw the fact to the attention of hon. members, that if we were dealing now with a manufacturing company some hon. gentlemen would have ample ground for denouncing all manner of crookedness, extortion and exploitation. I am not laying this to the charge of my hon. friends, but I simply say that if they ars going to attack the manufacturing interests of the country we will view their own operations and see whether or not the same general principles of finance are applied to their own business, and applied in a more successful manner than in the case of any manufacturing concern I know of. That being so, then I say to my hon. friends that they should withdraw the aspersions contained in their platform and in their speeches against the manufacturers.
I proceed a step further. I intimated this afternoon that my hon. friends opposite came to Ottawa-I think it was in 1910- and presented resolutions demanding that it be made a criminal offence to deal in futures on the grain exchange. We find this Grain Export Company, a subsidiary of the United Grain Growers, making a loss in one year of $245,000, a loss, according to the sworn statement o,f Mr. Rice Jones, due to the lack of sufficient margin in their gambling estimate of the matter. I am using

their own words that are crystallized into resolutions by these very gentlemen, and not my words. But in spite of that loss they succeeded in turning over to the parent company $300,000, and in paying a stock dividend of $150,000, and in addition to that, a year ago, they had $150,000 or $300,000 in .reserve-the secretary said he knew it was $150,000, and possibly it was $300,000. I say to hon. gentlemen who make charges of unreasonable profits against the whole World and particularly against the manufacturing interests, that we cannot find, in the wildest romance of manufacturing in this country, a more extreme type of profiteering than that.
Let us turn to another phase of their operations. I refer hon. members to a report laid on the table of the House last year to which I have already referred, namely, the report of Price, Waterhouse and Company, the auditors in connection with the elevators at the head of the Lakes. What do we find there? We find our friends, some of them in the House, operating a grain elevator leased from the Canadian Pacific Railway upon which they pay a rent equal to about six per cent, or seven per cent now, on cost of construction. On the operation of that elevator in one year they made a net profit of 211 per cent. Deducting from that profit of 211 per cent the losses they made on margins in speculating on grain that did not belong to them, it left 187 per cent. Why do I say speculating in grain that did not belong to them? This is a point which I wish the House to understand clearly. I could not emphasize it last year when I tried to place before the House the iniquitous character of this and other proceedings. It is contrary to an Act passed by this Parliament for any terminal elevator company at the head of the Lakes to deal in any grain overages in its care. The grain that is there is not their grain; they are not allowed to buy a bushel of grain; it is grain in transit; it is grain in trust. But the terminal elevators used to sell, in July or before the end of August, the anticipated overages. Once in a while they would get caught. One year the elevator of my hon. friends got caught and made one loss of, I think, $23,000 and another of a smaller amount. You may scrutinize with the utmost care the operations of my hon. friends in business and you will not find one single iota of deviation from the general methods of doing business by those whom they previously condemned. In issuing a pamphlet, and in subscribing to a platform of this kind,
they have no right to condemn those other operators when they are themselves indulging, infinitely more successfully, in the same practices and the same methods.
Going on a step farther, and coming to the parent company. This is a co-operative company. It was the father of this whole movement and the parent of this platform. That company has paid ten per cent since 1911, and it has an accumulated surplus of $1,700,000. It may be said, and it will be said if anybody chooses to reply to my remarks to-night, that there is a premium on the stock. According again to the sworn evidence of Mr. Rice-Jones a large portion of this premium on stock amounting to $400,000 was paid out in commissions for the sale of stock. That might reduce the $1,700,000 by $200,000, but after that is done you still have $1,500,000 of a surplus. That is a very handsome surplus. But that is not all of the story. The balance of the story is that in addition to the main operations of this concern there are branches such as the Grain Growers" Guide, a perfectly legitimate enterprise,, that make losses and have made losses for years and years. Those losses are hidden by and absorbed in the general prosperity of the company. The point in all this is that our hon. friends in advancing to this House and to the country this platform should delete all references carrying insinuations of corruption and insincerity on the part of their fellow-citizens, guilty as they are of exactly the same methods and practices but with enhanced success so far as results are concerned.
I find another plank in this platform; that in reference to the publication of election campaign fund contributions. I have no objection to that, I think it is perfectly proper. If I am not mistaken the Bill before the House is very clear on that point. It was introduced by this Government and we are supporting it. But let us examine this question of campaign funds. From one end of this country to the other speeches have been made. I have under my hand reports of speeches by the hon. the leader of the National Progressive party, the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in which he makes charges similar to those in the platform in referring to corruption in connection -with campaign funds.
Let me carry my hon. friends back in history about fifty or sixty years. The first lieutenant of the hon. member for Marquette is the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who, I am exceedingly sorrv to learn, is sick and in the hospital; I know

carelessly from the purely revenue standpoint. And so my hon. friends will find that in this Budget we are pretty well meeting the whole of this platform.
Now I wish to say a few words in connection with the Wheat Board. One criticism I have to make of the Wheat Board is that it is duplicating another board already in existence, namely the Grain Commission. I am not suggesting that in time of war it was not wise to appoint the Wheat Board, because under war conditions, under the exigencies of war, you are bound to do things which perhaps upon maturer thought in times of peace would not be done. The Wheat Board was appointed in war time. And now the war is over. The function of the Wheat Board is to market the wheat of Canada. I hold that it is an expensive luxury. I 'hold that if you are going to market wheat through governmental agencies, the Grain Commission can perform that function. If they are unable to do it-if the personnel of the Grain Commission is such that they do not understand the business of marketing this grain, then the commission might be enlarged for that purpose. But in connection with the .Wheat Board I find a situation that might well occupy the attention of the Government. For instance, the secretary, Mr. Young, is receiving $6,000 a year from the board. He is receiving an additional salary from the Lake Shippers' Clearance Association of $10,000. He is a pretty well paid official. I do not think, Sir, that he can successfully serve both masters; I do not think he can give to the country that impartial service wdiich such a commission, almost of a sacred character in its functions and duties if properly conceived, should give. Therefore I think the Government might well at a very early date consider the abolition of this board. It is a costly experiment and has served its purpose. The test is this: Did the Wheat Board lower the cost of marketing our wheat? I have gone into the case with considerable care, and I submit that it has not done so. I believe it was the intention of the Government that it should effect an economy in that direction. What are the facts? The bank interest and exchange in connection with wheat transactions is- exactly the same as it used to be; insurance- marine and fire-and storage, are still there under the Wheat Board as under private operation; freight, by land and by water is exactly the same. Now in regard to wheat that is sold direct to a country elevator, mark you, the Wheat Board has provided that there shall be a

margin allowed of from five to ten cents a bushel. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that these figures convey to hon. members an adequate idea of the magnitude of this margin. I am told by those who understand the business .and are familiar with its every angle that it means an average of between seven and eight cents a bushel on all the wheat that is handled in the West and, in fact, in the East too, I believe. Thalt margin is allowed where wheat is bought by the country elevators, and it is an extraordinary allowance. And, let it be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Riddell, the deputy chairman of the board, is the manager of three hundred of those country elevators, and that other interests represented on that board have under their direction another four or five hunderd. That hoard provides that the elevator carrying wheat through shall be paid from a certain period allowed by the Act-I think 15 days, which is covered by the first charge-until the wheat reaches its* destination at the head of the Lakes.

I would inform him that whenever he chooses to ask me any questions he will always find me willing to give him the floor, and I would suggest to him that that is a little item in the ethics of this House which it is always desirable to observe.
My statement, I reiterate, is absolutely accurate, and for the benefit of my hon. friend I will repeat it: That this Wheat Board, composed of gentlemen who largely control the line elevators of the prairies to the number of 800 or a thousand, provides a special storage charge, which is calculated from I think, the 15-day allowance in the original charge for handling until the wheat is landed at its point of destination at the head of the Lakes or at the mill, wherever it may be. And let me say this, Sir, that thalt storage, including the 8 cents a bushel I have referred to, has resulted in enormous earnings to these line elevators. My hon. friends talk about protect-

The farmers of the prairies do not realize the extent to which they are paying for this Co-operative Association, but the time has about arrived when they should know the actual facts in dollars and cents.
Now, on consigned wheat, mark you, going direct to the Grain Board-a transaction in which no other persons are doing *anything-that consigned 'wheat being shipped direct from the elevator to the Grain Board at the head of the Lakes, forsooth there comes in a one-cent brokerage charge, which goes to another party. Then *we find that the brokers at Winnipeg are taken care of, they receive t'heir fees just the same as if they were doing the business. We also find that the shippers and the exporters have their fees protected in the regulations of the Wheat Board-all at the expense of the farmer. I suppose my hon. friend will in a few minutes cite one of these items of ^ of a cent a bushel as a small item. But when we add these & and & and 1 cent, and 2 cents and 8 cents, in the aggregate they soon mount to a very handsome sum; .and then when we add to this 6 or 8 per cent which is deducted at the head of the Lakes and paid to the elevators of these gentlemen, the total amounts to a very considerable sum. Then they have provided for fees to the Lake Shippers' Clearance Association, of which forsooth this $6,000 and $10,000 secretary is an officer-one and the same individual-and is on this Wheat Board to see that the members of his association get their proper allowance. I do not say this in an unkind or critical spirit, but I suggest very seriously to the Government that it would be very desirable to have the audited statements and all other papers of the Wheat Board laid on the Table so that some of us, at any rate, might have an opportunity of examining them.
I find there is only one decrease-brokerage, reduced from * of a cent to & of a cent a bushel. I want to be perfectly frank, that is the only decrease that has been secured by the Wheat Export Board over private operation.
Now, I want to point out that the need of this Wheat Board passed with the signing of the Armistice. It never did lower the cost of handling our wheat; on the contrary, it enhanced that cost. I hold that after the term of this Wheat Board expires next August the marketing of our wheat should be left to the ordinary course of
trade. There is where I believe in the freedom of trade. And I would just like to pause a moment to give my hon. friend opposite a short dissertation on free trade.
The name free trade is an utter misnomer. Free trade started with the efforts of individuals centuries ago to get rid of embarrassing trade control. It was in the Hanseatic League and the free cities of Europe that freedom of trade first saw the light of day. The manufacturers," and shippers, and importers of those free cities found they were interfered with by the petty restrictions of feudal barons and despotic governments,' and they started a movement for the freedom of trade. In the early part of last century that movement developed in Great Britain into an attempt to free trade from the embarrassing restrictions which then hampered it. And so with regard to the Wheat Export Board, I would say to the House and to the Government, I believe absolutely in freeing our wheat business from this control. I believe absolutely in the freeing of our wheat business from control at this time. It may be said that I am giving voice to the opinion of an amateur. I refer the House to a recent report of one of the members of the Imperial Government who stated to the British House that after the most careful thought and study it was believed that the control of foodstuffs, the control of the purchase of wheat, had increased the cost of living, had increased the cost of food, and had in no way contributed to the welfare of the people at large.
Now, a word or two of a general character. This is a time when we should look facts in the face. There is no. use in blinding our eye.s to the fact that we have an enormous public debt. I was pleased when the Minister of Finance stated frankly to the House that it was useless to follow the custom that had been followed by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and by every other Finance Minister, that of giving the net debt. What we want to know is what our liabilities to the public are, and when we know that, we shall know what we are required to pay. As near as I can figure it from the statements which I have -secured, we have a debt of $2,500,000,000. That is what we have to take care of. We may have assets in addition to those which I have deducted from the gross debt, but they are not convertible. Mr. Speaker, I consider it a
privilege to have the honour of replying to the speech to which we have just listened, and which has been kept to the height of the high plane which this debate has maintained since its commencement, I will do my utmost not to lower that plane, and although I may differ from hon. gentlemen on the other side, I wish my Temarks t-o be taken as they are offered, and in the same spirit which animates me in making them.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) has divided his remarks into three parts, one of vdiich was a lecture that he thought it his duty to give to the Farmers' group. It is not my intention to interfere in that regard ; I will let the representatives of the Farmers' group settle their differences with the hon. gentleman. But may I be permitted to state that I was amazed to hear the hon. gentleman stating that the United Farmers were profiteers, and that their association was, in the question of overages, committing an illegal act. If 9 p.im. this be true, how is it that the Government supported by my hon. friend allows the United Farmers to be profiteers without taking them to task? And how is it that these United Farmers committing illegalities are permitted to continue committing illegalities and that the Government, which is responsible for those illegalities, still has the support of my hon.

friend? His position in this regard is not logical.
My hon. friend has taken a great deal of pains to show to the House and to the country that there was a contradiction between the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MeMaster). Any man belonging to a party and speaking in his individual name has a right to give his individual opinion; but if he belongs to a party and if he wishes to remain in that party, he must adhere to the platform of that party. The Liberal party held a convention in August of last year; they propounded their policy, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's and the hon. member for Brome, when they speak for the Liberal party, must adhere to that party's platform as propounded at that convention. But it is strange to me that my hon. friends would go to such pains to find contradictions in the policy propounded by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, when he himself declared to the House and to the country that he is going to support this Government which has no policy at all. What is the policy of the Government? Last year they promised the House and the country that there would be a general investigation into the affairs of the country and that revision of the tariff would take place. The hon. gentleman replies by saying: It is very fortunate for this country that this investigation was not held, because in the month of January the affairs of the world were more unstable than they ever were before. But he adds that he is glad to see that actually the situation in world affairs is now on a sounder basis. This is a poor answer. The pledge was given by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) during the first session of last year, and if the investigation had been carried on according to that promise, there would have been no necessity for the Government to do anything at the present session-at a time when, in the judgment of my hon. friend, the affairs of the world are in a better condition-other than to bring down legislation based on that investigation. But if the Government have had no policy-and the proof that they have no policy is that the ex-Minister of Finance promised last year that an investigation would be held and that a revision of the tariff would take place-in what situation are we this year? We are in actually the same situation. The new Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) says to the House: We are going to hold an investigation. Why? Because every one admits that

there is a feeling of unrest in this country as in the rest of the world; that something must be done. If my hon. friend is as pious and good as he wants us to be, I wonder why he supports a Government which, with their policy, have been unable to cure the unrest or to foster the best interests of this country? They have a policy of doing nothing; they have a policy of promising investigations, and all the while the unrest keeps on growing and growing every year. That is not extraordinary. Do you believe, Sir, that business men are going to put their money into undertakings when they do not know "what the policy of this Government will be? If you wish to have stability in this country, you must give to the trade, to the industries of Canada the assurance that they will not be disturbed. Otherwise they will stand back and wait, and when they wait the workingmen of this country are suffering more and more every day under the high cost of living; the people are suffering by reason of the taxation which is being imposed upon them and which is increasing year by year, and the capitalists of the country are afraid of the 'Government because they realize that although the Government are making a great cry that they have the confidence of the people, they have not that confidence as a matter of fact, and furthermore they do not deserve to have it, as I shall try to prove in the course of my remarks.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) says that the Wheat Board ought to be abolished because it was created as a war measure. Well, Sir, if that argument can be properly applied to the Wheat Board it is eminently more fitting to apply to the Government. They *were elected to win the w^ar and they pretend that they won the war, but after having won it they cannot restore peace in this country; and I really believe that as the Wheat Board ought to be abolished, so too should the Government be put out of existence, or at least, they should have a renewal of their mandate only if the people are willing to renew it. I believe that one fact that will not be disputed by any thinking person is this, that confidence is one of the basic essentials of human life; if you want to succeed you must have confidence in yourself, you must have confidence in your associates. But confidence, to be worth anything, must be reciprocal in character. And when I hear ministers saying that they trust the people, that have confidence in the people, I know but too well that they cannot add that they know that the people have confidence in them.

What have this Government done to win the confidence of the people? What have they done in their legislation, in their administration, and in the official declarations of the ministers of the Crown, and of their partisans? I believe that on this question of confidence we can derive some good lessons from the late war. The Allies won the war because there was mutual confidence between the commanding officer and the common soldier, and this confidence, mutual and reciprocal, created a unity of action. So long as we were not united in action, so long as unity had not been secured by any confidence of the Allies in one another, we must admit, our cause met with no great successes. Sir, this war has been marvellous from more than one standpoint. There is not a man, there is not an army corps, there is not a country that can rightly boast that the winning of the war was due to any single individual or nation. It was due to the concerted action of all of the Allies. The Allies were so united that they secured unity of action, which came from the confidence they had in one another. If I were permitted, I could give ar few examples to show what confidence did in the late war. When at the Battle of Mons the small "contemptible army" of Great Britain, as it -was named by the German war lords, sustained the orders and carried the fight in that murderous and atrocious retreat, every one admitted that that army was composed of heroes. But there are other examples. These British soldiers, having the fullest confidence in their commanding officers, remained at their posts because they knew that their officers would not permit a single sacrifice that was not necessary for the glory of the British arms. Take the example of the Argonne. When the Germans decided to crush Verdun, with the hope that the defeat of Verdun would mean the defeat of France before Great Britain could put forth all her effort to help France and before the United States could come to the rescue, what saved the situation? When the forts of Douaimont and Vaux were crumbling under the raging fire of the German artillery the French soldiers offered themselves as a living barrier to stem the wave of the German army, and they won the day because they had confidence in their commanding officers. It is the same in every phase of life. Now that the war is over every country must look to its own salvation, and it is the duty of a government to come to the rescue and save the situation. What has this Government done in
legislation and in administration, and what are the official declarations of its ministers?

Every nation of the
world is now seriously grappling with the problems which have been created by the war. Everybody knows I am not supporting the Government, but although I am opposing them I will not charge them with every possible crime, I want to give them credit whenever they deserve it. I am not going to charge them with being responsible, as some say they are, for the inflation of the Canadian currency. The problem of the present hour is the question of inflation. Some economists claim that inflation of currency has created the high cost of living. I believe with the Rt. Hon. Reginald McKenna and Professor Nicholson, of Edinburgh university, that instead of the high cost of living being the result of the inflation of currency inflation of currency is the cause of the high cost of living. This Government has done, on the question of the inflation of currency, as Governments have done all over the world.
After war was declared, and when, during forty-two months, 20,000,000 people were called to the colours, the rest of the world had to produce the food for these 20,000,000 men and the population back of the battle front. The men who responded to the call were the flower of the -world's manhood. During the long period of peace the world had accumulated an enormous reserve of goods of all kinds. When the soldiers went to the front they ceased to produce and they consumed ten, fifteen, or twenty times more than they were producing when they were at their work. We had to replace them by old men, young men, and women, all of whom have done their duty, but there was a loss of raw material, there was a loss of time, there was a higher cost of production. There was a higher cost of production also because the purchasing agents of Europe were coming to this country and buying at any price at all all kinds of goods that we could supply. All that we could produce was bought in advance at higher and higher prices. The consumer at home had to pay these new prices. Inflation of the cost of living brought about inflation of wages. The working men could not live on the wages they were earning before the war and wage scales had to be readjusted.

I do not know. What brought this to my attention, Sir, was. a statement on the financial page of the Montreal Gazette of Monday last, where it was shown that the gold holdings of Canada were in the proportion of approximately 32 per cent of its currency. The next day I was amazed to hear the Minister of Finance state to the House and to the country that .our gold reserve was 43 per cent. I have much confidence in the Minister of Finance -and I have much confidence in the Montreal Gazette. That journal to my mind could not have printed that statement without the knowledge, officially or officiously, of the Government. I look again at the public documents, and here is what I find [DOT]as stated by the Minister of Finance: That our Dominion note currency on the 31st of March, 1920, was $311,932,791; ourgoldhold-ings at the same date were $100,286,280. Therefore, according to his own figures, our gold holdings would be approximately as the Gazette states, 32 per cent. But by what operation did the Minister of Finance put the figure at 43 per cent? He calculated the gold reserve of the banks with the gold holdings in the central gold reserves. But, first of all, from the total circulation of the paper money of the Dominion and of the banks he had taken off $97,700,000, the statement reading, " Less Dominion notes held in Central Gold Reserves, $97,700,000." I admit, Sir, that according to financiers our gold reserve should be at least 40 per cent. But when we take in the whole issue of our paper currency, we must balance it with the total gold reserves held by the Government, and nothing else. Why should the Government Compute the gold held by the banks as security for their own note issue so as to depreciate the difference between their circulation and their gold holdings? Furthermore, why should the Government be al-

lowed to take out of its note issue $97,700,000 of paper money and deposit it in the Central Gold Reserves?
Well, Sir, if such a statement as that can be published broadcast by the Minister of Finance, I say that the Government do not trust the people. Why do they not state our financial position frankly? At the time of the war there was no secret made of it; every one knew' what v'as the situation. Every time the Government appealed to the people, whether to secure men, whether to. secure credit, or whether to secure endorsement of certain legislation, they got everything they asked for. The Government had received a mandate to w'in the war, and in execution of that mandate they could ask for anything they wanted, and they were sure to get it, for the people had confidence in them. Why not proceed in the same manner to-day and tell the people frankly what is our position? Every one knows that we have an inflated currency; every one know's that it will have to be deflated; and before assuming the heavy burden of taxation that the Government intend to put on the shoulders of the people the situation should be frankly stated to the country. And it is not good management on the part of the present Administration to curtail the gold deposits of our banks in an attempt to show that our inflated currency is less inflated than it really is.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take up so much time, and I will conclude with these few words. I would say to the Government: Stop the profiteers and you will strike at the root of the high cost of living; there is no other way. You cannot instantly deflate your currency because it would mean ruin to the country; but strike .at. the very root of the, . evil and you will cure the unrest which that evil engenders. I say again: Reduce the tariff and you will help to reduce the cost of living. The policy followed by this Administration has had the result of creating an unrest which continues to grow every day and every week, and this policy is proved by its results to be wrong. Change it; reduce the tariff, and you will reduce the cost of living. Be prepared to recall your inflated currency according to a gradual and progressive method and come back as soon as you can to a sound gold basis. Trust the people, lead them wisely and firmly; enact legislation which will appeal to them; give to this country that management of national affairs which will appeal to the electors, and you will regain their confidence. It is the bounden duty of

the Government to secure peace, and to command the confidence of the people, and this you cannot do if you continue your present policy of legislation and administration and of making official declarations which at sight do not correspond with the official figures that are given to the country.
Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM (Peterborough West):	Mr. Speaker, in speaking well of
the Budget I should like also, 'before going on, to refer in as complimentary a way as possible to the speech of the bon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) and that of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). The member for St. Hyacinthe, on rising, expressed a desire to maintain the high plane reached by the member for Vancouver. I can assure him that before he sat down he had reached that high plane; he furnished us with as much argument as any man possibly could furnish hostile to this admirable Budget.
It .must 'be remembered, in criticizing this Government for having no policy, that their policy for years has been that of war, and on the return of peace it was necessary for them to formulate a peace policy. This peace policy has been formulated and announced in the Budget, and it is the most admirable combination of protection and free trade that a man could possibly wish for. I do not think that any Budget that was ever announced in the Parliament of Canada has secured the commendation and praise from the people of Canada that this one has. Everybody was curious to know how in the face of the universal high cost of living and general taxation the Minister of Finance would secure the necessary revenue through taxes to carry on; but he has surprised us all, not only by securing the necessary taxes, but by doing it in such an easy, offhand manner that it is doubtful if it will be felt at all by the people. No more skilful handling of finances could, in my humble judgment, possibly be imagined, and every praise should be accorded to the minister for his most admirable work.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville has told us that there is serious' unrest in the country. He did not compare Canada with other countries; if he had done so he would have seen, and we all would have seen, that the unrest in Canada was as nothing in comparison with the unrest in other countries, Britain and the United States included. If we had had in proportion to population the fatal clashes between the people and the military that have occurred in the United States, there 166
would have been calls and cries for special sessions and the very winds of Heaven would have been called to the aid of the Opposition, as has so frequently been the case in their denunciation of this Government. But in Canada there has been nothing worthy of the name, except, perhaps, a little centre of disturbance here and there. The unrest in this country is a minimum; certainly a minimum in comparison with the unrest in other countries. In all fairness, due allowance should be made for that, and observations and criticism should be tempered accordingly.
This Budget has the honour of giving birth to the newest and biggest party that ever arose in Canada, the People's party of Canada. We have the Liberal party, the Progressive party and the People's party. We do not wish in future that there should occur in the councils of Canada what has occurred in the legislature of Ontario, where a party 245,000 votes in the minority undertake to govern the province. The Liberal party are proud of their old record, and well they might be. The Liberal party, successor to the Whig party, was founded upon freedom and it has more or less maintained that tradition to the present day. It is the one great merit of the Liberal party that it stands for more or less of the great principles of freedom. But it has received a serious set-back. It has been divided, and out of its rib has been created the Farmers' party of Canada. At the next election the contest will be between the People's party and the Farmers' party.
